title: The righteous guarded by fear of God amid enemies
english: For those from circumcision despise him, because with unforgetting memory he keeps the ordinances of God (Psalm 118:162 [119:162]).

The saying also has David’s own particular meaning: when he was pursued by Saul without cause and out of envy, his fear of God restrained him from taking vengeance. But it extends also to the common case, that there is no other way to escape wars of princes unharmed unless one is guarded by the fear of God.
After the gift of wisdom he asks again for salvation from dangers. This too is a reward for his willing zeal for the divine law (Psalm 118:173 [119:173]).

So then he was truly saying just now that he awaited eternal salvation, and now also, longing for it, he has made this the goal of his study of the law. For he says that he will live again and praise God, helped toward this by his all-wise judgments. This is Christ, who comes down in place of human beings to the saving death for human beings, and by his suffering redeems those in sufferings, and by his death redeems the dying. And in accordance with this there follows, “My soul will live,” and what comes after (Psalm 118:175 [119:175]).

This was so immediately after the first apostasy of the human being, when Cain by deceit struck down his brother, and it is so throughout the whole present age, as is shown in other cases and in the present matter. So the person who looks to God, worn down and afflicted by this, asks for salvation from him. He does not foresee the cessation that will come then, when he is brought up to dwell in the peaceful city, with good and bad alike sharing its citizenship.

Another passage also indicates the foreign land in one respect, into which Israel fell and sojourned, and that his sojourning was extended to the greatest length. Prophesying in lament he brings this out so that it reaches also to the present condition; for this is the longest sojourning.

For the good and godly keep peace as far as depends on them and with all human beings, whenever there is no need of judicial punishment such as God commanded against the Canaanites and Amorites, forbidding friendship with them. But the wicked and those who do not know God would never enter into friendship with the good; rather they abhor godliness, and they do not receive kindly anything good from the godly, nor are they tamed by their kindness.
He calls mountains here the invisible and heavenly powers. And while he awaits help through them, he says that the help does not originate from them but from the Creator (Psalm 120:1b-2 [121:1b-2]).

It is a joy to hear what is said by the angels, clearly the ones who speak to the prophets and who, as it were, lead the herd of Israel. Such is the one made known through Zechariah, interceding for fallen Jerusalem and speaking of her future dwelling. The psalmist says that he rejoiced when he heard these things, and that he foresaw the secure dwelling in the holy city and, as it were, perceived the matter as present prophetically. For this is what “Our feet were standing in the courts of Jerusalem” means (Psalm 121:1b-4 [122:1b-4]). The standing of feet is the immovable dwelling which the holy prophets also proclaim. The opposite of this was when, according to the history, God shook the foot of Jerusalem from its own land. So the psalmist speaks of the rebuilding of the city, seen by him as also by Ezekiel, and says that the building is of a city united—not, clearly, in the customary way of walls uniting it, but of the inhabitants united to one another. Therefore he did not say “city” but “as a city” having its joining together at once. For neither Ezekiel nor Zechariah declares that it will be inhabited under walls, but unwalled, and that its wall will be the Lord, since God is the guardian and holder together of the unity of the saints. He interprets the unity as being through the inhabitants themselves, saying, “For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, a testimony to Israel, to give thanks to the name of the Lord.” Not because walls were thrown around them were they united, but because they themselves were united through themselves. It is a testimony to Israel, clearly witnessing to the truth of the promises, and to give thanks to the name of the Lord, because confession of grace is owed by the beneficiaries to the one who fulfilled the wonderful promise.

orientation: Apollinaris is commenting on Psalm 118 (119) and the opening verses of the Songs of Ascents, explaining how the psalmist's words apply both to David's own trials and to the church's present afflictions.

title: Thrones of David's house and the true building of God
english: He says that thrones of the house of David were established in her, since Daniel also prophesies a kingdom over all things. It is not the rule of some one person or of a single ruler, but a common kingdom for the best and most godly, through whom the kingdom of David is set upright by the grace of Christ, who gave to the twelve apostles the right to sit on twelve thrones and judge Israel.

But he will not allow good subjects to be corrupted by evil demons. Rather, after the good have toiled a little under them, he will free them from a harmful slavery that does not dare to come upon those who are ruled by God.

Solomon is inscribed on the song, because he built the temple. But it signifies the true Solomon, our Lord, the cause of the true and peaceful building. For this reason the building is shown to be made by God, and its guard is secure because it is guarded according to God. And this is fitting, because the buildings and guards made by human beings fell into vanity: the night watches of those who keep guard, and the diligent and laborious care by day. For this reason human things, being such as they are, came first, so that divine things alone might be recognized as having what is sure and unchangeable. Just as righteousness came through the law, so that God's righteousness might be seen after it as having what is genuine and alone true, and true life after the life that was in shadow and image.
"When he gives sleep to his beloved ones." He has indicated the rest from God that is like sleep and will be given out of love.

"For I have stretched you, Judah," he says, "for myself as a bow." Here too he calls the remaining saints the arrows of the Mighty One, for the defeat of the ungodly and those who are violent with injustice.

The paths of entrance are many and various, and the lives of those who begin are of many kinds, but there is one perfection that reaches the height. He characterizes those who fear the Lord by saying next what sort of people they are: "Those who walk in his ways." For those who do not do this do not fear the Lord. The fear of the Lord is a turning away from evils, and the one who has turned away from evils is ready for the divine ways.

The cry "out of the depths" could mean out of the waters of afflictions that have poured around him. The endurance and the repetition of the same words belong to one who clings and hangs on and does not wish to let go of his supplication because of his desire. For this reason he says, "Hear my voice, and let your ears be attentive."

The place did not become clear to David from the matter itself by his own forethought. For this reason he says, "We heard and we found," because a command of God pointed out the threshing floor of Ornan, on which he built the altar to turn away the death that was destroying the generation of the Hebrews. And having loved the discovery exceedingly, as one who had come to know what he had long desired, he rejoices in the matter and loves the worship there. There, he says, God also made a visitation, because the glory of God became manifest through the presence of the angel.
In the same way, he says, he foretells the time of Solomon, in which the ark is moved from the tent and set in the temple, and divine glory appeared and a cloud filled the house.
These things, he says, we see happened in Solomon's time according to David's words.

For the favor is toward David, even if the benefit extends to those after him. Just as it is said directly to Solomon that because of David he would not fall entirely from the kingdom, so also the sparing for David's sake passed to his descendants, just as it is said to Hezekiah: "I will shield this city for the sake of David my servant."

To the earlier and brief gifts he brings the greatest one, which preserves all of them. For from the beginning he gave an abundance of food, which one translator calls "prey" and another renders as "grain." And he promises to make the inhabitants free from want. Concerning priests and holy ones he has made a decree that they be saved and attend to the sacred hymns. But when all these things had already been corrupted—the nation unable to enjoy the good things of the land because it had fallen under the power of the Romans, the priesthood failing, and all the joy in the temple dissolved—the great power arose there, the horn of David, which gores every power of enemies, a beautiful lamp shining with heavenly light for David and for his offspring, who, having begun there, sends out his radiance to the whole world, as the prophet Simeon says: "A light for revelation to the nations and for glory to your people Israel."

The ointment was also a parable of a divine matter, but what comes from God is made more evident by the parable of the dew that comes down from heaven upon the mountains. For the gift and the good are heavenly, not human, and do not appear among human beings apart from the gift from above.

title: Hymns, wonders, and the true God
english: He signals beforehand the work of hymns that will take place at the gathering together of all the saints, when neither day nor night will it cease, since sleep itself will not prevail in the power of the incorruptible and untiring bodies of that time.

Hymns are the end of good things, and the subject matter of hymns is the works of God, his gifts and benefits. Those who hymn are not strangers standing far off, but attendants who remain near, just as David appointed the singers to remain for this purpose.

One might say that a great benefit, and the chief of all benefits from God, is the making of humans his own, just as he made the people of the Hebrews his own and set them as exceptional for himself beyond all the nations at that time, placing them as something more and superior, inasmuch as the God of all is his own God to them in intimacy, though in creation he is God of all.

Remembering the wonders that happened around Israel—things not done by the nature that appeared at the beginning, but by a will beyond nature, some heavenly, such as fire and hail and darkness, some earthly, such as frogs and locusts and gnats and the punishing power against the firstborn, and some done in the sea and the deep, such as the things at the Red Sea—he brings them back to the creative authority, joining these to those as having come from the same power, saying that he is the one who once for all lifts up clouds from the ends of the earth and flashes forth lightnings as the prelude of rains and sends out winds from an unseen source. They are not known where they are before they blow. He says that the unseen and unknown origin of the winds is God's treasury, the winds being understood to be stored away somewhere continually, as in the treasuries of bodies.

He indicates that the wonders did not happen for Israel alone, but for the knowledge of God through all the earth and all time—not only while the works were being done was the doer known, but also afterward through memory.

Above, then, he called them gods according to the custom of the nations, though they are not gods. Now, to shame the falsely named gods, he calls them idols, discrediting them by the material, because they are silver and gold, and by the workmanship, because they are made by humans, and by the lifelessness along with the vanity of the likeness of souls, because there is no spirit of life in them. All these things carry the open discredit of the worship and the open refutation of the demons, that those whose likenesses are such things are not gods. For the likeness of God is divine; therefore the human being who is an image is the divine one, not the one deprived of the Godhead.

No less than the subduing of those who warred against them, the feeding in the desert and the guiding of them without want, and the destruction of the kings of the Amorites, he sets down as a demonstration of God's mercy, who gave their land to the Hebrews as a good land to dwell in. And this was the treasuring up for the righteous of the wealth of the impious. For they would not have perished otherwise, had they not come to the fullness of their sins, as God said to Abraham. And Moses says that Israel did not take possession of their land because of his own righteousness, but because of their lawlessness and because of God's love for the fathers. So against those the destructive judgment was just, while toward these the beneficent gift was loving, and the piety of the fathers became a preparation for sharing in that love. For in this way the things from God are shown forth justly and well and fittingly for the world.
He makes clear that they will be in a desert, like the condition of captives after their removal from their own cities. For this is what it means: "On the willows we hung up our instruments."

And according to the spiritual worship, they considered the foreign souls a foreign land, and they guarded against bringing out the divine things among them, as things being moved from their own place into a foreign one, as the divine mouth of Christ says: "Do not give what is holy to the dogs, and do not throw your pearls before the pigs." Such was Herod, who wanted to see the signs of Christ, not seeking this for reverence but for pleasant spectacle, and therefore he did not obtain it.
